title: The road so far, and the detours.
lead: Everything we have built and learned, one line per track. The grey crosses are ideas we tried and dropped, and we wrote down why, so you don't have to repeat them.

days.title: The start

days.title: Thinking big

days.title: Looking around

events.title: V0 thumb and index printed
events.note: The first prototype: 8 joints, tendon-driven, 3D printed.

events.title: Tendons cross each joint on its axis
events.note: New routing for the index knuckle and middle joint, designed in CAD (not printed yet).

events.title: 21 joints, 21 servos
events.note: The first V1 plan: one servo for every joint.
events.why: Every servo draws current and takes space in the forearm. Twenty-one of them needed a huge power supply and left no room for the tendon channels.
events.lesson: Count the power and the space before you count the joints.

events.title: V1: five fingers, servos in the forearm
events.note: The full hand designed in CAD, with human finger proportions.

events.title: A 5-joint thumb
events.note: We added a fifth thumb joint, like a human thumb, and removed it a day later.
events.why: The extra joint needed another hinge and more tendon channels in the most crowded part of the hand. It was not worth the complexity for a first full hand.
events.lesson: Copy the human hand where it matters, not everywhere at once.

events.title: Back to a 4-joint thumb
events.note: A simpler thumb, with the tendon routing reworked.

events.title: 5 mm spool for the index knuckle
events.note: The knuckle bent easily but extended weakly. A smaller spool pulls twice as hard.

events.title: 16 servos for 20 joints
events.note: Each finger's last joint follows the middle joint, so it needs no servo.

events.title: Coupling the fingertip with a tendon
events.note: The first idea for making the fingertip joint follow the middle joint: a second tendon.
events.why: A tendon has to be tensioned, stretches over time and goes slack. The fingertip joint has no servo of its own to pull the slack out.
events.lesson: When nothing can take up slack, use something stiff.

events.title: Coupling with a rigid bar
events.note: A small bar per finger keeps the fingertip within 0.6 degrees of the target.

events.title: The finger linkage modelled in CAD
events.note: Bars and plates for all four fingers, with no collisions.

events.title: Firmware v0.1 for 8 steppers
events.note: Smooth speed-up and slow-down, motors switch off when idle, text protocol over USB.

events.title: Steppers as the final motor
events.note: Cheap stepper motors drove the first prototype. We decided V1 would not use them.
events.why: A stepper has no idea where it is, so someone must straighten the hand by hand before every start. Eight of them also use up nearly every pin on the controller.
events.lesson: Position feedback is worth paying for.

events.title: Smart-servo driver
events.note: Feetech SCS0009 on one shared bus, with position feedback.

events.title: First V0 test rig
events.note: The index finger wired to an ESP32-S3.

events.title: Firmware 0.4.0 for 16 servos
events.note: Torque off at boot, nothing moves before a command.

events.title: First MuJoCo model
events.note: Converted from the CAD export, checked against the real hand.

events.title: Python library and digital twin
events.note: One Hand interface for the simulation and the real hand.

events.title: Webcam control of the hand
events.note: Your own hand moves the simulated one.

events.title: V1 model with 20 joints
events.note: Every tendon is simulated.

events.title: 36 tendons and the finger linkage
events.note: The simulation matches the 16-servo design.

events.title: A simulated arm
events.note: OpenArm's shoulder and elbow stand in until we build our own.

events.title: Two arms, mirrored left hand
events.note: The first body: two arms on a pole.

events.title: AI research hub and the big goal
events.note: A robot that does what humans do, with the hand as the focus.

events.title: Grasp learning system
events.note: Reinforcement learning in simulation, with a human-like reward.

events.title: Reward hacking: hovering beat winning
events.note: The first reward ended the episode on success.
events.why: The robot learned that hovering just below the success height scored more than finishing, because finishing ended the game. A learner finds every loophole in its reward.
events.lesson: Read what your reward really pays for, not what you meant it to pay for.

events.title: A reward that pays for holding
events.note: Success no longer ends the episode, so holding the object is what counts.

events.title: Study of the best robot hands
events.note: The biggest gap: fingertip force.

events.title: 77% grasp success in 49 minutes
events.note: A cloud GPU, simulating many hands at once. It used the older hand design, so we will repeat it.

events.title: Training the hand on the arm
events.note: The arm brings the hand to the object (about 87%).

events.why: It felt cold and nerdy. The project wants to be friendly to anyone who is curious, not only to engineers.
events.lesson: Design for the person you want to invite in.
